content.title: About
content.content: Eggs are a widely consumed food, most often from chickens, though duck, quail, and goose eggs are also eaten in many regions. They have been part of human diets for thousands of years. An egg consists of a firm shell, a protein-rich white, and a yolk that contains most of the fat and many of the vitamins and minerals. Eggs are eaten boiled, fried, scrambled, baked, or used as an ingredient in countless dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shell color (white, brown, or blue-green) depends on the breed of the hen and does not reflect nutritional value.
The egg white and the yolk contain different nutrients: the white is mostly protein and water, while the yolk holds fats, vitamins, and minerals.
A hen typically lays no more than about one egg per day.
Eggs act as a binder, thickener, and leavening agent in cooking and baking.
Quail, duck, and goose eggs are popular in many national cuisines.

items.title: Source of high-quality protein
items.content: Eggs provide complete protein containing all essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Eggs are one of the richer food sources of choline, a nutrient involved in normal cell function.

items.title: Provides vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2), vitamin A, and small amounts of vitamin D.

items.title: Contains eye-supporting carotenoids
items.content: Egg yolks contain lutein and zeaxanthin, plant pigments associated with eye health.

items.title: May help you feel full
items.content: Protein-rich meals such as those with eggs may increase the feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Egg allergy is among the more common food allergies, especially in children.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Raw or undercooked eggs may carry Salmonella. Pregnant women, young children, older adults, and people with weakened immunity should avoid them.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain dietary cholesterol. People with certain health conditions should ask a healthcare professional how many eggs are suitable for them.

items.title: Biotin absorption
items.content: Raw egg whites contain avidin, which can bind biotin. Cooking eliminates this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eggs can be boiled, poached, fried, scrambled, or baked in omelets, casseroles, and pastries. They are also added to salads, sandwiches, soups, and sauces. Cook eggs until the white is set and the yolk is firm to reduce the risk of foodborne illness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggs in the refrigerator in their original carton, away from strong-smelling foods. Raw eggs in the shell usually keep for several weeks when refrigerated. Hard-boiled eggs should be refrigerated and eaten within about a week. Do not use cracked or dirty eggs.

content.title: About
content.content: Garlic bread with parmesan is a slice of bread topped with a blend of butter, minced garlic and grated parmesan, flash‑frozen for long‑term storage. When baked, it develops a crisp golden crust and a fragrant, slightly cheesy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen garlic bread can be kept for up to 12 months without quality loss.
The parmesan used is typically aged at least 12 months, giving it a distinct nutty aroma.
Traditional Italian “bruschetta” often features garlic and cheese; this product is a modern adaptation.
Quick preparation: just 8‑10 minutes in a preheated oven at 200 °C.
Garlic contains allicin, a compound with antibacterial properties.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Garlic provides sulfur compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Moderate regular garlic intake may help lower blood pressure.

items.title: Source of calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Parmesan contributes significant calcium and phosphorus for bone health.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: The cheese adds both dairy and plant‑based protein, promoting satiety.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The product contains no added sugars, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Parmesan may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and added salt increase sodium levels; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Garlic sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience heartburn or gas after consuming garlic.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Frozen bread with butter and cheese is calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake the bread in a preheated oven at 200 °C for 8‑10 minutes until golden and crisp. Serve hot as a snack, optionally sprinkling extra fresh herbs or parmesan. It can also be used as a base for sandwiches or served alongside soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen garlic bread in its original packaging in the freezer at –18 °C. Once thawed, bake immediately to retain crispness. Do not store the thawed product at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Halva is an eastern sweet made from ground roasted seeds or nuts (sunflower, sesame, peanuts) and sugar or honey caramel. It has a crumbly, slightly fibrous texture and a rich nutty flavor. Halva is eaten as a treat with tea and coffee and added to desserts and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word halva comes from an Arabic word meaning sweet.
In Turkey, the Middle East, and Central Asia, halva made from tahini, or sesame paste, is common.
In Russia and the CIS countries, sunflower halva is especially popular.
Halva comes with nuts, cocoa, vanilla, and other additions.
For a light texture, a decoction of soapwort or licorice root is sometimes used in production.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Halva is high in calories and gives quick energy.

items.title: Contains plant fats and protein
items.content: The seeds and nuts used to make halva contain healthy fats and plant protein.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Sunflower halva provides vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contains calcium and magnesium
items.content: Sesame halva provides calcium, magnesium, and other minerals.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: Sesame and sunflower seeds provide small amounts of these minerals.

items.title: Calories and sugar
items.content: Halva is very high in calories (about 500 kcal per 100 g) and contains a lot of sugar, so portions should be small, and it is worth brushing your teeth.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Sesame, sunflower, peanuts, and nuts are common allergens, and halva can cause severe reactions.

items.title: Diabetes
items.content: People with diabetes should eat halva with caution and count its carbohydrates.

items.title: Ingredients
items.content: Some halva contains palm oil, flavorings, and other additives, so read the ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Halva is best eaten in small pieces, for example one or two slices, with tea or coffee. Cut it with a sharp knife, and add it to ice cream, yogurt, porridge, desserts, and baked goods. Choose halva with a simple ingredient list.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store halva in a cool, dark, dry place in a sealed package. In hot weather oil may seep out of it, and in a humid environment it crumbles or spoils. After opening, wrap it in cling film. Discard halva that smells rancid or is moldy.

manicotti-vegetable-and-cheese-filled-wi.title: Manicotti, vegetable- and cheese-filled, with tomato sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Manicotti are large tube-shaped pasta shells stuffed with a mixture of vegetables (usually zucchini, spinach, carrot) and cheese (mozzarella, ricotta). They are served in a flavorful tomato sauce. The dish is completely meat‑free and suitable for vegetarians.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tubular shape of manicotti holds the filling well, making it a favorite in Italian cuisine.
Traditional filling uses ricotta and spinach, but modern versions incorporate a variety of vegetables.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are often San Marzano varieties, known for their sweet flavor.
The dish is commonly served in family‑style restaurants as a “home‑cooked” pasta.

items.title: Rich in vegetables
items.content: The vegetable filling provides vitamins A, C and dietary fiber, supporting immunity and digestion.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with meat‑based pastas, this dish contains less saturated fat, which is heart‑friendly.

items.title: Plant‑based protein
items.content: Vegetables and cheese together supply a complete set of amino acids for vegetarians.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables aid the absorption of nutrients.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; choose a low‑sodium version if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional manicotti are made from wheat flour and contain gluten, which can be problematic for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve manicotti hot, drizzled with extra tomato sauce. They pair well with grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or a drizzle of olive oil. Ideal as a main course or part of a vegetarian lunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. Uncooked manicotti should be stored in a cool, dry place for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled sausage is a cooked or smoked meat sausage that has been cured in a brine with spices, vinegar, and sometimes sugar. The process gives it a distinctive tangy‑salty flavor, aromatic notes from the spices, and a longer shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of pickling sausages originated in Eastern Europe, where cold climates made brining a practical preservation method.
Typical brine ingredients include mustard seeds, coriander, garlic, and bay leaf, creating a complex aroma.
Pickled sausage can be either boiled or smoked; smoking adds a subtle smoky depth.
In some regions it is served cold as an appetizer, while in others it is heated and used in hot dishes.
There are many regional variants that differ in spice blends and marinating time.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The sausage provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat in the sausage supplies heme iron, which supports healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Processing retains B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins that are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Zinc and phosphorus are present, contributing to immune health and bone strength.

items.title: Probiotic effect (when fermented)
items.content: If the brine contains live cultures, they may help maintain a healthy gut microbiota.

items.title: High salt content
items.content: Pickling requires a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Nitrites and preservatives
items.content: Some varieties contain nitrites that can form potentially harmful compounds over long storage.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain meats (e.g., pork) may experience reactions.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The sausage can be high in saturated fats, so it should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled sausage can be enjoyed cold as a snack, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, soups, or stir‑fries. It is often lightly pan‑seared before serving to enhance its aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the pickled sausage in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C, either in its original brine or in an airtight container. For longer storage (over 2‑3 weeks) keep it submerged in fresh brine, changing the liquid every few days. Discard the product if it develops an off‑odor, discoloration, or a slimy surface.
